p: Herodotus, the Greek historian whom Cicero called the father of history and others have called the father of lies, visited Egypt about two thousand three hundred years ago, and remarked that the country was the gift of the river. He was right. Egypt is a desert, the largest of deserts, through which runs a single river, the Nile, bordered by a narrow strip of black and fertile land, never more than a few miles wide, until near the sea the river spreads into the great fan of its delta. Every summer, before the building of the great dams in the century to come, the Nile rose, swollen by the rains of Ethiopia far to the south, and covered its valley with water and rich mud, and then fell, leaving the soil watered and fertilised for the year's sowing. The Egyptians called their land Kemet, the black land, after that mud, and the desert they called the red land.

No other civilisation has lasted so long. From the uniting of Upper and Lower Egypt under a single king, about three thousand one hundred years before Christ, to the death of Cleopatra in thirty years before Christ, is three thousand years: a span longer than that which separates Cleopatra from ourselves. Through all that time, with interruptions, the Egyptians were ruled by Pharaohs who were regarded as gods upon earth, spoke a single language, worshipped largely the same gods, and wrote in the same hieroglyphs. Their stability is almost incomprehensible to a modern European, whose maps are redrawn every generation.

Historians divide this long story into periods of strength, which they call the Old, Middle and New Kingdoms, separated by intervals of weakness and disorder which they call the Intermediate Periods. This scheme was invented by modern scholars and is a little too tidy, but it serves.

The Old Kingdom, from about two thousand seven hundred years before Christ, was the age of the pyramids. The Great Pyramid at Giza, built for the Pharaoh Khufu, whom the Greeks called Cheops, about four and a half thousand years ago, was the tallest building in the world for nearly four thousand years, until it was overtopped by the spire of Lincoln Cathedral in the fourteenth century. It contains some two million three hundred thousand blocks of stone. It was not built by slaves, as Herodotus supposed and as a great many sermons have repeated, but, as the Encyclopaedia reports from the discoveries of the twentieth century, by organised gangs of paid and fed workmen, whose village, bakeries and graves have been found nearby, and who scrawled on the stones the names of their gangs, such as friends of Khufu. They were conscripts, very probably, and their labour was a form of tax; but they were not chattels.

The Middle Kingdom, from about two thousand years before Christ, was an age of good government and fine literature, including stories and moral teachings that read with surprising freshness. The New Kingdom, from about one thousand five hundred and fifty years before Christ, was the age of empire, when Egyptian armies with their chariots marched into Syria and Nubia, and the Pharaohs filled the temple of Karnak at Thebes with monuments to their own victories. To this age belong the most famous names: the female Pharaoh Hatshepsut; Akhenaten, who tried to make his people worship a single god, the disk of the sun, and was execrated for it after his death; his young successor Tutankhamun, a minor king whose tomb the men of the next century will find almost undisturbed, in nineteen twenty-two, and whose golden treasures will make him the most famous Egyptian of all; and Ramesses the Second, the great builder, who reigned for sixty-six years and fathered, it is said, more than a hundred children.

The Egyptians had a great many gods, often shown with the heads of animals: Horus with the head of a falcon, Anubis of a jackal, Thoth of an ibis. To a Greek or a Roman, and still more to a Hebrew or a Christian, this seemed bizarre. I do not think it was. The animal heads were ways of showing the character and power of a god, much as our heralds put lions and eagles upon a coat of arms.

What has most struck every visitor is the Egyptian concern with death. The tombs, the mummies, the elaborate books of spells to guide the soul through the underworld, all suggest a people obsessed with the grave. But the Egyptians were in fact obsessed with life, and wished it to continue. The paintings in their tombs show feasting, hunting, farming and music, the pleasures of this world, which the dead expected to enjoy in the next. To reach that happy state, the soul had to pass a judgement, in which its heart was weighed in a balance against a feather, the symbol of truth and justice. If the heart was heavy with wrongdoing, it was devoured by a monster. It is an image of moral seriousness that need not shame any faith.

For fourteen centuries after the last hieroglyph was carved, nobody could read them. Learned men of the Renaissance supposed them to be mystical symbols containing the secret wisdom of the ancients. The key was found in seventeen ninety-nine by French soldiers of General Bonaparte's expedition, at a place in the delta called Rosetta: a stone bearing the same decree in hieroglyphs, in a later Egyptian script, and in Greek. It passed to the British Museum as a spoil of war, where you may see it today. Using it, a young Englishman, Dr Thomas Young, made a beginning, and a brilliant Frenchman, Jean-François Champollion, announced in eighteen twenty-two that he had deciphered the system. He showed that the hieroglyphs were not mystical symbols at all, but a writing that recorded the Egyptian language, partly by sounds and partly by pictures. The secret wisdom of the ancients turned out, in large part, to be lists of offerings and the titles of officials. It is a fate that awaits all our archives.
